soil-water-180.title: How rain soaks into the ground, and when it stops
soil-water-180.text: Sand and well-aggregated soils can take in 2.5 cm of rain an hour, while high-clay soils accept as little as 0.25 cm. That intake is infiltration, the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil. Gravity drives it, helped by capillary forces, absorption and osmosis. Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate, usually given in meters per day. It lasts only while there is room at the surface, which depends on porosity and on how fast earlier water moves down through the {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. As a storm goes on, that room shrinks. Infiltrated water fills storage and weakens capillary pull. Wetted clays swell and narrow their pores. Raindrops striking bare ground wash fine particles into surface pores. Robert E. Horton suggested that capacity drops quickly early in a storm, then settles to a near-constant value after a couple of hours. When rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in, the surplus usually runs off, unless a physical barrier holds it in place. Rates are measured in the field with devices such as {{ref:soil-water-187}}, permeameters and rainfall simulators.

soil-water-191.title: Permeability: how freely fluids slip through porous ground
soil-water-191.text: Well-sorted gravel is among the most pervious natural materials; unweathered clay and fresh granite are among the least. Permeability, usually written k, measures how readily a fluid, gas or liquid, flows through a porous material such as rock or soil. It depends on {{ref:soil-phys-063}}, but also on the shapes of the pores, how well they connect and the pressure inside the material. Its SI unit is the square meter. The practical unit, {{ref:soil-water-203}}, is about 10−12 m² and honors the engineer Henry Darcy. Most materials range from a fraction of a millidarcy to several thousand; unconsolidated sands may exceed 5000. Intrinsic permeability belongs to the solid skeleton alone, whatever the fluid, and forms one part of {{ref:soil-water-193}}. Keeping the two apart lets engineers allow for temperature effects on viscosity and for fluids such as brines or petroleum. Permeability matters for groundwater, oil and gas reservoirs, filtration and judging ground for construction.

soil-water-164.title: Water content, from bone dry to every pore full
soil-water-164.text: A soil's water content runs on a scale from 0, when it is completely dry, up to its {{ref:soil-phys-063}}, when every pore is full. Water content is the quantity of water a material holds; in soil it is called {{ref:soil-water-155}}. It can be given by volume, as volumetric water content, written θ, or by mass, as gravimetric water content. Soil science, like geotechnics, gives the gravimetric figure relative to the sample's dry weight. Multiplying it by the bulk specific gravity converts it to volume. Most soils hold less water than their porosity allows, which is what unsaturated means. Water content also changes what soil is: solid, semi-solid, plastic or liquid. The water contents at which it changes state are the Atterberg limits. How much moisture varies from spot to spot depends on climate. It rises with overall wetness in semiarid regions, falls with it in humid ones and peaks at intermediate wetness in temperate ones.

soil-water-155.title: Soil moisture, the quarter of a loam that keeps plants alive
soil-water-155.text: Half of a loam's volume is solid. Gas fills a quarter and water the other quarter, and only about half of that water is available to most plants. The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight, is soil moisture. It shapes soil formation, structure, stability and erosion, but its main importance is for plant growth. Water makes up 80–95% of a plant's protoplasm. It carries nutrients as a solvent and keeps plants upright through turgor, the pressure of water inside their cells. Water leaves a field in four ways: as runoff across the surface, as water draining through the soil, by evaporation from the surface and by transpiration from plants. Inside the soil it moves under gravity, osmosis and capillarity. Entering water drives air out of the largest pores and can burst air-filled aggregates, a process called slaking. Roots empty the largest pores first. Water in the smallest pores clings so tightly to particles that roots cannot take it, so availability depends strongly on texture. Moving water also dissolves solutes and colloids and redeposits them lower in the profile, a process called leaching. Probes such as {{ref:soil-water-225}} and {{ref:soil-water-170}} measure soil moisture in place, and remote sensing estimates it from afar.

soil-water-214.title: Drainage, from Mohenjo-daro's houses to French drains
soil-water-214.text: Every house in the major Indus Valley cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro had water and drainage. Drainage is the natural or artificial removal of surface and subsurface water from an area that has too much of it. The internal drainage of most farm soils keeps them from staying severely soaked. Many still need artificial drainage to raise production or manage water supplies. The invention of hollow-pipe drainage is credited to Sir Hugh Dalrymple, who died in 1753. Simple open drains, pipes and berms remain common, alongside larger earthworks and newer technologies. Surface drains carry runoff from paved ground. Subsurface drains remove water seeping into the soil, and the commonest type is the French drain, a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe. Drainage protects structures too. Behind an impermeable retaining wall, undrained groundwater builds hydrostatic pressure. That pressure can crack the wall and wash out soil, leaving voids and sinkholes. Most jurisdictions have a body of drainage law limiting how far a landowner may alter the drainage from a parcel.

soil-water-193.title: Hydraulic conductivity, the measure of how fast water moves
soil-water-193.text: A well sunk into sand and gravel draws water far more easily than one in clay or unfractured granite. The difference is hydraulic conductivity, written K: how easily water moves through a material's pores or fractures, in meters per second. K depends on the material's intrinsic {{ref:soil-water-191}}, on how saturated it is, and on the density and viscosity of the fluid. Formally, it is the ratio of volume flux to hydraulic gradient, the flow per unit area divided by the slope that drives it. Saturated hydraulic conductivity, Ksat, describes flow through saturated material. Natural values span many orders of magnitude, often in a lognormal pattern, and vary greatly from place to place. Direction matters: vertical K can be orders of magnitude below horizontal K. So does scale, since testing a cubic meter of an aquifer, a water-bearing layer, generally gives a different answer from a cubic centimeter sample. In unsaturated soil, K depends non-linearly on {{ref:soil-water-164}}. One material's unsaturated K spans a wider range than saturated K does across all materials. K is estimated from grain-size and pore-size distributions and texture, or measured in laboratory and field tests interpreted with {{ref:soil-water-201}}.

soil-water-172.title: Water potential: why water flows from soil to sky
soil-water-172.text: Water climbs from soil into roots, up a stem, out through the leaves and into the air without any pump. Each step has a more negative water potential than the one before, so the water flows passively. Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions. In soils the reference is usually pure water at the soil surface. Written with the Greek letter ψ, it expresses water's tendency to move because of osmosis, gravity, mechanical pressure and matrix effects such as capillary action. Unrestricted water moves from higher to lower potential. Dissolved solutes lower the potential; added pressure raises it. In soil, total potential sums three parts: {{ref:soil-water-173}} from capillary action, an osmotic part in saline soil and a gravitational part that drives downward flow. A saturated soil sits at 0 kPa. After free drainage, at {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is −33 kPa, and at the {{ref:soil-water-178}} −1500 kPa. Dry air is typically about −100 MPa. No single instrument covers the whole range. Electrical resistance blocks read from −90 to −1500 kPa, while {{ref:soil-water-223}} reaches −10,000 kPa.

soil-water-153.title: Soil water retention: holding water against gravity
soil-water-153.text: In temperate Victoria, Australia, water stored in wet winters carries most perennial plants through dry summers. That reserve depends on soil water retention, a soil's ability to take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity. Soils keep absorbing until they are full, or until their pores cannot pass water on fast enough. Some water drains by gravity to streams, but much stays, and plants and other organisms use much of what stays. Particle size sets the pattern. Water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water and sands let it pass. Clay type, organic content and {{ref:soil-phys-001}} also matter. An agricultural topsoil is roughly 25% water, 25% air, 45% mineral and 5% other, though its water ranges from about 1% to 90%. Water neither held nor used can sink to {{ref:soil-water-247}} as recharge. Saturated soils can even fail by mass movement, so soil water concerns geotechnicians and soil conservationists alike.

soil-water-201.title: Darcy's law, born in the sand filters of Dijon
soil-water-201.text: From the 1830s the engineer Henry Darcy studied water flowing through sand filters, hoping to improve the water supply of Dijon, France. In 1856 he published the result in a construction report. Darcy's law is an equation describing the flow of a fluid through a porous medium, and it became the basis of hydrogeology. Like Ohm's law for electricity, it makes flow rate proportional to a difference, here in hydraulic head. Hydraulic conductivity plays the part of electrical conductivity. Flow rises with the medium's permeability, its cross-section and the pressure drop. It falls with the fluid's viscosity and the length of the path. Without a pressure gradient nothing flows. The Darcy flux is a flow per unit area, not the speed of water in the pores; porosity links the two. The law holds only for slow, smooth, laminar flow, as in most groundwater, at Reynolds numbers below one, and up to 10 in tests. Very coarse sediments may flow turbulently and escape it.

soil-water-175.title: The water retention curve, a soil's moisture signature
soil-water-175.text: In 1907 Edgar Buckingham filled soil columns 48 inches tall with six soils, from sand to clay, and drew the first water retention curve. The curve links a soil's water content to its {{ref:soil-water-172}}. Also called the soil moisture characteristic, it differs between soil types and predicts water storage, plant water supply and aggregate stability. Near zero potential the soil is almost saturated and holds water mainly by capillarity. As it dries, the remaining water is bound ever more strongly, in the smallest pores, at grain contacts and as adsorbed films. Sandy soils release most of their water at higher potentials. Clayey soils, which also bind water by adhesion and osmosis, release it only at lower ones. At any given potential, peaty soils usually hold far more water than clayey soils, and clayey soils more than sandy ones. Even one soil has two curves. Pores fill and drain differently, so hysteresis, a lag between wetting and drying, gives separate wetting and drying curves.

soil-water-247.title: The water table, where saturated ground begins
soil-water-247.text: In the Nile Delta, wheat tolerates a water table 45 cm below the surface, while cotton needs 90 cm. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation. Below it, pores and fractures are full of groundwater; above it lies the unsaturated zone. It sits where water pressure equals atmospheric pressure. In soils with strong capillarity, water is drawn up above it in a damp band. The level rises and falls with rain and with water lost by evaporation and plants. In Britain or California it is lower in summer, and the band between levels is the zone of intermittent saturation. It is rarely flat. Its slope, the hydraulic gradient, depends on recharge, withdrawal and permeability. Where it meets the surface, springs, rivers and lakes appear, and groundwater inflow sustains their base flow. A perched water table sits above the regional one, on an impermeable or slowly permeable layer. A well in a confined aquifer shows a potentiometric surface instead.

soil-water-189.title: Macropores, the soil's fast lanes for water and air
soil-water-189.text: An earthworm burrow is a fast lane for water. In soil, a macropore is any cavity larger than 75 μm. Macropores lie between peds, the natural clumps of soil, and between large sand or gravel grains. Wet–dry and freeze–thaw cycles crack soil into them. Those made by roots and organisms such as earthworms are called biopores. Water moves freely under gravity in macropores but is held by capillarity in micropores. So macropores raise hydraulic conductivity and carry fast flow along preferred paths, and water infiltrates and drains quickly. They aid recharge and gas exchange with the air, but they can also wash nitrate from fertilizers into groundwater. Their formation generally decreases with depth, as the processes behind it weaken. {{ref:soil-agri-095}} and compaction easily alter them. Compacted forest landings have little macroporosity, and added {{ref:soil-bio-114}} can improve it. Chemists use the word differently, for cavities larger than 50 nm in porous solids.

soil-found-094.title: Hollows that hold back the flood
soil-found-094.text: Every pit and hollow in a field is a small reservoir. Depression storage capacity is the ability of land to hold water in its pits and depressions so that it does not flow away. Together with infiltration capacity, it governs Horton overland flow. Once both are exceeded, water flows across the land, possibly causing flooding and erosion. Its study matters in geology and ecology, and above all in hydrology.

soil-water-187.title: Infiltrometers: rings driven into the ground
soil-water-187.text: The simplest infiltrometer is a metal ring driven into the soil and filled with water. The device measures the rate at which water infiltrates soil or another porous medium. Common types include single-ring and {{ref:soil-water-188}} designs, {{ref:soil-water-204}} instruments and falling-head infiltrometers. A single ring can be fed at constant head, a steady depth of water, often from {{ref:soil-water-244}}. Or the level is left to fall while the operator records how much water enters. Holding the head constant makes the supply rate equal the infiltration capacity, and the rate of entry relates to the soil's hydraulic conductivity. Rings have flaws. Driving one in deforms the soil, and a single ring lets water spread sideways. Rings cannot reliably represent furrow, sprinkler or rain infiltration. They measure only ponded, saturated flow, which macropores dominate wherever they are distinct.

soil-water-181.title: Why litter, cracks and roots speed water into soil
soil-water-181.text: On sandy loam, infiltration under leaf litter can be nine times that of bare ground. Bare soil forms a crust or surface seal that keeps it low. Rainfall, soil and surface conditions together control how fast water enters a soil. Rain infiltrates faster than snow or sleet. Entry is rapid early in a storm, while the soil is unsaturated, and slows as it saturates. Dry soils have the highest capacity, partly saturated soils a moderate one, and saturated soils no room for more. Fine-pored clays take water more slowly than coarse sands, except dry clays, which crack and take it quickly. Compaction lowers porosity and so capacity. After wildfires, water-repellent soils can cut infiltration sharply or stop it. Roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed it. With no vegetation, rates can be very low, causing excess runoff and erosion. Pavement prevents infiltration, and steeper slopes shed water faster. Alkali soils have poor structure, so rainwater ponds and evaporates before crops can use it.

soil-water-182.title: Calculating infiltration, from simple sums to supercomputing
soil-water-182.text: Infiltration is one term in the hydrologic budget, so if every other term is known, simple algebra gives it. Infiltration equations are methods for estimating the volume and rate of water entering a soil. The rigorous standard is a numerical solution of {{ref:soil-water-238}}, coupling groundwater and surface water through non-uniform soil. That solution is computationally expensive, not guaranteed to converge, and sometimes struggles to conserve mass. A newer approach, {{ref:soil-water-239}}, replaces it with three ordinary differential equations that always converge and conserve mass. It assumes vertical flow and uniform layers. For deep, well-drained soil that starts evenly moist, good approximate methods give the infiltration for a single rain event. At the simple end, a stripped-down use of Darcy's law assumes the gradient acts over an arbitrary length and ignores cumulative depth. Many argue it is too simple to use.

soil-water-205.title: Pedotransfer functions: turning cheap data into costly answers
soil-water-205.text: In 1989 Johan Bouma coined a name for "translating data we have into what we need". A pedotransfer function, or PTF, is a predictive function that estimates soil properties from {{ref:soil-agri-082}} data. The idea is older than the name. In 1907 Briggs and McLane gave the wilting coefficient as 0.01 sand + 0.12 silt + 0.57 clay. In the 1960s Salter and Williams linked texture classes and particle-size distribution to the water a soil can hold for plants. PTFs turn readily available data, such as field morphology, texture, structure and pH, into estimates of properties that are laborious and costly to measure. Most work has targeted the water retention curve and hydraulic conductivity, which have large databases. PTFs are empirical, built with regression and data mining. The USDA's ROSETTA program applies them with neural networks.

soil-water-160.title: A rye plant's 10,620 kilometers of root hairs
soil-water-160.text: A single winter rye plant, grown four months in 0.0283 cubic meters of loam, formed 620 km of roots and 10,620 km of root hairs. Yet it touched only 1.2% of the soil volume. Roots grow into new soil every day, so the volume they explore, and the water they take up, grows greatly over a season. Plant water uptake is how plants draw soil water into their roots. Most of it is passive. As water transpires from the leaves, it pulls the whole column of sap in the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, up from the roots. The cohesion-tension theory describes this pull. Osmosis adds a push: salts concentrated in roots draw water in. That matters most when transpiration is low, at night or in high humidity. The root endodermis and leaf stomata regulate the upward flow, and cavitation in the xylem can break it. Root architecture, the layout of the root system, helps plants adapt to the soil's water and nutrient supply. Some roots even re-wet dry soil. Shortage costs yield: grain sorghum held at 1300 kPa soil suction from seed-head emergence to seed set lost 34% of its production.

soil-water-178.title: The permanent wilting point, past which plants cannot recover
soil-water-178.text: Keep a wilted plant in a saturated atmosphere for 12 hours. If it still cannot regain turgor, its soil has reached the permanent wilting point. That is the lowest soil water content a plant needs in order not to wilt. By convention, following {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, it is the water content at −1,500 kPa, or −15 bar, of suction. It roughly marks the boundary between available and unavailable water. There seeds will not germinate, and plants wilt and die unless adapted to recover. Closing stomata can slow transpiration and delay wilting, especially in drought-adapted plants. In 1912 Briggs and Shantz proposed the wilting coefficient, the water content at which plants first wilt beyond recovery without added water. Veihmeyer and Hendrickson of UC Davis found it to be a constant of the soil, whatever the conditions. Experiments by Richards and colleagues fixed today's limits for plant growth: −1/3 bar at {{ref:soil-water-177}} and −15 bar at the wilting point.

soil-water-161.title: Evapotranspiration, the soil's great return to the sky
soil-water-161.text: Of all the water a plant uses, only 0.1% to 1% stays inside it; transpiration carries off the rest. Evapotranspiration is the combined movement of water into the atmosphere from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants. Evaporation moves water straight to the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration carries it from the roots through the plant and out of the stomata as vapor. Together they return, on average, three-fifths to three-quarters of the precipitation that falls on land. Three things mainly control the flow: water available in soil and water bodies, the energy in air and soil, and the atmosphere's capacity to take up moisture. Drier soil means less evapotranspiration and a warmer soil surface. Where {{ref:soil-water-246}} exceeds rainfall, soil dries out unless irrigated. The flow is counted in millimeters of water over a set time. It is measured directly with a weighing {{ref:soil-water-248}}, or estimated from a catchment water balance, an energy balance or weather data. With infiltration, deep leakage beyond the roots and runoff, it is one of four main parts of the water balance at a point. It can also concentrate the salts in irrigation water to toxic levels.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated flow pushes water; unsaturated flow pulls it
soil-water-156.text: Unsaturated flow moves water at most about 2.5 cm a day. So roots cannot wait for water to come to them; they keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. Water moves through soil in two modes. Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to {{ref:soil-water-177}}, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. This is saturated flow. At higher suctions, water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient. It pulls water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores: unsaturated flow. As soil dries, its connected wet pathways shrink, so unsaturated hydraulic conductivity falls in a very non-linear way. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, {{ref:soil-bio-114}}, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present and how warm the soil is. Warm soils take in water faster. Frozen soils, including permanently frozen ground, may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. {{ref:soil-water-238}} gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-231.title: Impervious surfaces: when the city seals the soil
soil-water-231.text: In dense city centers, over 90 percent of the ground is sealed. Impervious surfaces are ground covered by water-resistant materials such as asphalt, concrete, brick or stone, mainly pavements and rooftops. Soils compacted by urban development are highly impervious too. Cover climbs with urbanization, from one or two percent in rural areas and about 10 percent in low-density suburbs to over 70 percent in industrial areas. Paving ends rainwater infiltration and natural recharge, which can cause urban flooding, and starves tree roots of air. Porous pavements, green roofs and infiltration basins make cities behave more like pervious soil.

soil-water-168.title: Measuring soil moisture without digging it up
soil-water-168.text: Soil moisture can now be gauged by a probe in one field or by satellite imagery combined with hydrological models. Soil moisture measurement means estimating water content in place, instead of drying samples. Several geophysical methods do it, among them {{ref:soil-water-223}}, {{ref:soil-water-170}}, {{ref:soil-water-226}} and {{ref:soil-water-225}}. Others include amplitude domain reflectometry, electrical resistivity tomography and ground-penetrating radar. Geophysical sensors often monitor soil moisture continuously for agriculture and research. Each method has strengths and weaknesses, so combining techniques can reduce the drawbacks of any one. Some farmers now schedule irrigation from these readings, a practice called smart irrigation.

soil-water-223.title: Timing an electrical echo to read soil water
soil-water-223.text: The same technique that locates a fault in a kilometer-long cable, to within centimeters and without digging, can measure the water in soil. Time-domain reflectometry sends an electrical pulse along a line and reads its reflections. Wherever the impedance along a conductor changes, part of the signal reflects back, and the return time gives the distance to that change. In soil, the pulse's speed depends mainly on the permittivity of the surrounding material, its response to an electric field. Permittivity varies greatly with moisture and temperature. Hoekstra and Delaney (1974) and Topp et al. (1980) showed that it is closely tied to water content. The probe is two or more parallel metal rods, typically 10 to 30 cm long, linked to the instrument by coaxial cable. Probes at several depths record when wetting arrives after rain starts, giving the speed of infiltration.

soil-water-218.title: Waterlogging: when soil drowns the roots it feeds
soil-water-218.text: Badly run irrigation has waterlogged over 2 million hectares of Pakistan's Indus Plains and 2.19 million ha of Indian canal commands. Waterlogging is the saturation of soil with water, so that its air is restricted and anaerobic, oxygen-free, conditions prevail much of the time. All plants need oxygen to respire, and waterlogging usually blocks air from reaching the roots. Apart from rice, most crops, such as maize and potato, are highly intolerant of it. Prolonged waterlogging harms the roots of mesophytes, plants of moderately moist ground. The reducing subsoil drives {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, methane production and the reduction of iron and manganese oxides. Roots can survive by forming aerenchyma, air channels in their tissue, by switching to anaerobic metabolism and by changing their architecture. In irrigated land, salinity often follows, because waterlogged soils stop the salts brought by irrigation water from being leached out.

soil-water-228.title: Holding the water table at the right depth
soil-water-228.text: Wheat in the Nile Delta tolerates a water table 45 cm down; cotton there is sensitive and needs 90 cm. Watertable control holds the water table at a chosen height by means of drainage. On farms it raises crop yields. In cities it protects building foundations, underground transit and buried utilities. Subsurface drainage keeps once-waterlogged land at a depth that suits its use. A shallower permitted depth makes a system cheaper, but lowering the water table has side effects whose costs must be counted. Shallow open ditches gave way around 1900 to buried clay tiles about 30 cm long, and from 1960 to corrugated plastic pipes laid by trenching machines. Pumped wells give vertical drainage and can be spaced over 1000 m apart, against 100 m or less for pipes and ditches. Many large projects were over-designed and ignored environmental side effects, which gave land drainage a poor reputation. Drainage also helps control salinity, and hydraulic conductivity weighs heavily in its design.

soil-water-215.title: Draining farmland, from Dutch steam pumps to Florida citrus
soil-water-215.text: In the Netherlands, 15th-century windpumps could drain only marginal land. The Haarlemmermeer had to wait for large steam pumps, which drained it between 1849 and 1852. Agricultural land drainage removes excess water from farmland, from wetland soils to fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged. Clay-rich soils pass water down very slowly, and hardpans or shallow rock block it. When excess water shuts out air, roots suffocate. Even excellent soils waterlogged for a week of the year can lose their fruit trees. Ditches turned glacial marshes in the northern United States and Europe into mucklands for vegetables and other high-value crops. Florida's flatwoods citrus groves are pumped after heavy rain. Rice needs complete water control, since fields are flooded or drained at different stages. Evapotranspiration concentrates the salts in irrigation water, so irrigated land may need periodic over-irrigation and drainage. Acid sulfate soils are an exception: subsurface drainage is normally not advisable, though surface drainage in rainy periods can help reclaim them.

openers.water-in-soil: Water decides much of what a soil can do, and this chapter follows it from the surface downward. It begins with infiltration, the process by which water on the ground enters the soil, and with the quantity a soil then holds. Some soils take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity; others let it pass quickly through their pores and cracks. One equation, first written for beds of sand, describes how easily water flows through them; another measure describes how hard the soil pulls on the water that stays. Where there is too much, drainage removes it, and deeper down lies a surface below which the ground is fully saturated.
